opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came from being nervous. The lottery ticket hypothesis made a strong claim: inside these big, randomly initialized networks there are small subnetworks that, trained in isolation from their original initialization, can match the full network's accuracy. When you say something like that, the first reaction from a skeptical reader, and I was the most skeptical reader, is "what did you do to make that happen?"

There are many knobs in deep learning that can quietly produce a result. Learning rate schedules, warmup, the exact pruning scheme, how many epochs you train, which layers you prune, whether you tuned hyperparameters on the test set. Any of those could create an effect that looks profound but is really an artifact of one particular setup. I didn't want the finding to rest on a trick I'd stumbled into. I wanted it to be about neural networks, not about my training script.

So I tried to keep things as vanilla as possible. I used standard architectures and standard training setups, the kind people would recognize, and I tried not to introduce new machinery whose only purpose was making the result look better. When I did have to make choices, I tried to be upfront about them and show what happened when you changed them. The random reinitialization control is a good example. If you take the same sparse structure and give it a fresh random initialization, does it still work? If it did, the "lottery ticket" story would be wrong, and it would just be about the architecture of the mask. The controls were there to rule out the boring explanations.

There's also a broader motivation. Our field moves fast, and a lot of papers report results that don't survive contact with a slightly different setting. I'd been through enough of that, reading papers, trying to reproduce them, and finding the effect evaporated, that I didn't want to add to the pile. If people were going to spend time building on this idea, I owed it to them to make sure the foundation wasn't something I'd accidentally manufactured.

And frankly, that caution paid off in an interesting way. When we scaled up to bigger networks like ResNets on ImageNet, the original procedure didn't work as cleanly. Because I'd tried to be careful about what was and wasn't doing the work, it was easier to see that something was different and dig in, which led to the later work on rewinding to early in training rather than all the way to initialization. If I'd papered over things with clever design choices, I think I'd have understood a lot less about what was going on.

r001.rationale: The response says a skeptical reader might ask what the authors did to produce the result, and explains that seemingly minor training and pruning choices could create an apparent effect that was really an artifact. This conveys why those choices could raise suspicions about the work.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing people forget about the lottery ticket paper is that I was a first-year grad student when I started it. I didn't have a reputation to fall back on, and I knew the claim we were making was going to sound a little too good. "There's a small subnetwork hiding inside this big network that trains just as well on its own." That's the kind of result where, if you're a skeptical reader, your first instinct is to go looking for the trick. And honestly, that's the right instinct. I'd have done the same thing.

So a lot of my energy went into asking, what's the version of this experiment where someone can't say "well, you just cheated"? If we only showed one architecture, people would say it's an artifact of that architecture. If we only showed one pruning method, they'd say it's the pruning method. If we reinitialized the weights randomly and it still worked, then the whole "winning ticket" framing is just a fancy way of saying sparse networks train fine, which was already known. So the random reinitialization control wasn't a nice-to-have, it was the entire point. The initialization is the claim. Without that comparison there's no paper.

The other piece was being honest about where it broke. Early on, the simple one-shot version didn't scale to the deeper networks. We could have quietly buried that in an appendix or picked hyperparameters until it looked clean. Instead we said, look, iterative pruning is required here, and here's the learning rate warmup hack we needed on ResNet, and we're not fully sure why. That felt uncomfortable at the time, but it turned out to be the most useful part, because it pointed straight at the follow-up work on rewinding and stability that actually explained what was going on.

I think the deeper reason I cared is that I came in from a background where I'd watched a lot of empirical ML results fail to replicate, and I didn't want to add one more to the pile. I'd much rather publish a smaller claim that holds up than a big one that gets a lot of attention and then quietly erodes. If the result is real, the controls only make it stronger. If it's not real, I'd rather find out myself than have someone else find out for me.

r001.rationale: The response says skeptical readers would look for a trick and explains how choices such as architecture, pruning method, and reinitialization controls could make the result seem like an artifact or an unsupported claim.

astra-6.text:
Because we were making a pretty surprising claim: that you could find a small network inside a randomly initialized network that, trained on its own, could match the original network’s performance. I wanted people to be able to take that claim seriously without getting hung up on whether some unusual choice in our experiments was responsible for the result.

Every experiment involves choices, but if you’re introducing a new idea, it helps to keep everything around it as straightforward as possible. Then the discussion can focus on whether the phenomenon is real and what it means. That was the motivation: make the evidence as clean and convincing as we could.

r001.rationale: The response says unusual experimental choices might distract people or make them question whether a choice caused the result. It does not clearly say reviewers might suspect deeper problems in the work.

sol-6.1.text: I wanted the result to be convincing. We were making a pretty surprising claim: that you could find a small subnetwork inside a randomly initialized network that would train well on its own. And I didn’t want that claim to depend on some unusual experimental choice, where someone could reasonably say, “Well, maybe it only works because you did that.” So the idea was to keep the setup as straightforward as possible and remove alternative explanations. If people were going to be surprised, I wanted them to be surprised by the result, rather than distracted by how we got there.

r001.rationale: The response says unusual experimental choices might make someone think the result depended on those choices, but it does not communicate that minor design choices could lead reviewers to suspect deeper problems in the work.
